description: I'm a grade 7 student from Lahore Pakistan. I am deeply interested in space missions and space exploration, my goal with this challenge is to make an app which can seamlessly train a junior astronaut for his mission in the space.
summary:
A day in life of an astronaut is an interactive browser game that puts players in charge of a four-person research station near the Moon’s south pole. Players choose an astronaut, listen to their crewmates, and make decisions about oxygen, water, food, power, repairs, crops, research, and emergencies across three missions.

We developed a story-led simulation. The station’s systems are connected: producing oxygen uses water and electricity; recycling water requires power and maintenance; and scientific work competes with survival needs. A guided first shift teaches these relationships one step at a time, while NASA and NTRS resources support the scientific ideas and are clearly separated from gameplay simplifications.

The project addresses the challenge by letting future junior astronauts practice the same habits used in mission planning: systems thinking, prioritization, teamwork, and risk management. This matters because space exploration depends not only on individual technologies, but also on understanding how every decision affects people and the wider mission.
details:
A day in life of an astronaut is an interactive browser game for young players, especially ages 9–14. The player joins a four-person crew at a fictional research station near the Moon’s south pole. They choose which astronaut to play, listen to advice from the other crew members, and make the final decisions that keep the mission running.


The game contains three missions of increasing difficulty. Players manage oxygen, water, food, battery power, crew health, equipment condition, crops, spare parts, and scientific research. These are not separate scores: they form one connected simulation. For example, the oxygen generator needs both water and electricity, the water recycler needs power and maintenance, and the greenhouse uses water and energy to produce food. Players can set power priorities, repair equipment, assign crew members to different jobs, prepare the radiation shelter, and respond to emergencies.

The experience begins as a guided story. The mission clock stays paused while ORBIT, the in-game assistant, introduces one control at a time. Later, the player can ask the crew for suggestions whenever they need direction. Emergencies also pause the clock and present three crew opinions with different costs, benefits, and risks. Safer choices receive clear positive feedback, while risky decisions show their consequences without pretending there was always one perfect answer.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes systems engineering understandable through play. Instead of asking children to memorize facts, it gives them a safe place to test ideas, see cause and effect, make mistakes, and recover. Players practice reading trends, setting priorities, comparing trade-offs, working with limited supplies, and considering how a technical decision affects people.


Our intended impact is to help young learners see themselves as future astronauts, scientists, engineers, and mission planners. We also want the game to be useful for families, classrooms, science centers, and STEM clubs. A complete mission takes roughly 8–15 minutes, so it can support a short demonstration or a longer discussion about closed-loop life support, energy storage, radiation safety, space agriculture, teamwork, and resilience.


The game runs in an ordinary modern web browser and does not require an account, internet service, paid API, or high-end computer. This makes it easier to share in classrooms and events with limited equipment. Player progress is stored only in the local browser, which also avoids collecting personal information.

Tools and technology

We developed the project with using Superintelligence for coding:

- HTML5 for the game’s screens, controls, dialogs, and accessible structure.

- CSS3 for the responsive layout, visual design, transitions, and reduced-motion support.

- Modern JavaScript for the game engine, story flow, crew decisions, resource simulation, saving, and interface behavior.

- HTML Canvas for the animated lunar landscape and cutaway station, including moving astronauts, equipment, plants, lighting, and environmental effects.

- Web Audio for locally generated interface sounds without external audio files.

- Node.js and its built-in test tools to test mission rules, emergencies, resource behavior, saving, progression, and complete winning strategies.

What makes the project creative

Many educational space projects present facts as a quiz or show resources as unrelated bars. A day in life of an astronaut turns the station into a causal network. A decision can protect one resource while spending another, and the same choice can be sensible in one situation but dangerous in a different station state.

The playable-crew structure also makes technical decisions feel human. Maya, Idris, Sofia, and Eli notice different parts of a problem based on their roles in command, systems, biology, and medicine. Their suggestions are not simply right or wrong; they help the player compare safety, research, supplies, and long-term resilience. The story-led introduction makes this complexity approachable without removing meaningful choices.

The visual station is generated with code rather than assembled from downloaded images. Players can see astronauts move to their assignments, plants grow, equipment operate, doors open, supplies change, and emergencies affect the base. This connects the underlying simulation to a visible place and crew.

Factors the team considered

We considered scientific credibility, accessibility, age-appropriate learning, performance, and honest communication about the model. NASA and NASA Technical Reports Server resources informed the relationships among oxygen, water recovery, lunar power, radiation, crops, and the lunar environment. At the same time, the game clearly labels compressed time, accelerated crop growth, abstract radiation points, and other educational simplifications.

We designed the interface so important information is communicated with words and shapes as well as color. Controls have keyboard focus states, the layout adapts to smaller screens, sound is optional, and nonessential animation respects reduced-motion preferences. We also considered beginner confidence: the first mission teaches one action at a time, the clock can always be paused, and the crew provides support without solving the game for the player.
